candidates.title: Beyond Model Choice: A Harness-Centered Framework for Designing Clinical Large Language Model Agents
candidates.abstract: Clinical large language model agents depend on both model capability and the surrounding system that selects information, constrains actions, and verifies execution. In this Viewpoint, we argue that this harness should be an explicit unit of clinical agent design, evaluation, and reporting. Our aim is to help clinical informatics and development teams specify this layer and to help evaluators and institutional governance teams assess its contributions and risks. Selected benchmarks show substantial performance differences across harness configurations, but architecture comparisons, bundled improvements, and within-model component comparisons support different levels of causal attribution. We propose a revisable 3-tier framework: tier 1 specifies general orchestration functions, including prompts, tools, output schemas, control flow, memory, and generic verification; tier 2 specifies their clinical adaptations for knowledge integration, differential reasoning, missingness and temporality, safety verification, and workflow alignment; and tier 3 specifies a failure-driven evaluation cycle applied to both. Our contribution is a framework that makes these connections explicit. We provide classification rules, an illustrative clinical example, a proposed evaluation protocol, and a minimum reporting checklist. Observable execution traces are distinguished from private model reasoning, with provenance and privacy safeguards supporting retrospective reconstruction. Evaluation should separate task success, clinical correctness, process safety, and operational reliability. Lightweight fine-tuning can complement harness design; their interaction requires controlled study. The framework is a proposal for empirical testing, not a validated taxonomy or evidence of deployment safety.

candidates.title: Learning to remember: advances in memory mechanisms for large language models
candidates.abstract: Abstract Memory has become a central mechanism for extending large language models (LLMs) beyond fixed context windows, stateless interaction, and static parametric knowledge. This survey organizes the literature around three complementary dimensions: the life cycle of memory, the storage substrate, and the system role that memory plays in LLM-based agents, while using cognitive-science-inspired memory concepts as a lightweight conceptual motivation rather than as a separate technical contribution or implementation family. On this basis, we distinguish three mechanism families: nonparametric memory, where information is stored outside model parameters in text, graph, multimodal, or database-like structures; parametric memory, where information is stored or accessed through activations, key-value caches, learned modules, adapter-based parameterizations, or model weights; and memory for agent evolution, where stored experiences support reinforcement learning, continual learning, procedural reuse, context engineering, and agent harness design. Evaluation is treated as a separate cross-cutting component rather than as a memory mechanism. Unlike surveys that focus primarily on retrieval-augmented generation or long-context modeling, this paper emphasizes the full memory life cycle: construction, maintenance, retrieval, consolidation, forgetting, governance, and evaluation. By aligning conceptual motivations, computational memory mechanisms, benchmarks, and deployment concerns, the survey provides a structured roadmap for designing memory-augmented LLM agents that are persistent, adaptive, auditable, and safe to update over time.

candidates.title: A Comprehensive Survey of Retrieval-Augmented Generation: From Foundations to Frontiers
candidates.abstract: Large Language Models demonstrate strong generative capabilities but remain constrained by static training data, susceptibility to hallucination, and an inability to access current or domain-specific information at inference time. RetrievalAugmented Generation (RAG) addresses these limitations by coupling language models with external retrieval mechanisms that dynamically supply relevant knowledge during generation. In the years since its introduction, RAG has expanded from a single architecture into a broad ecosystem of retrieval modalities, architectural variants, and deployment patterns that is increasingly difficult to navigate. This survey provides a unified treatment of that landscape, organized around five retrieval paradigms: sparse lexical retrieval, structured data retrieval, dense semantic retrieval, graph-enhanced retrieval, and agentic retrieval. For each paradigm, we trace the evolution from foundational concepts to current practice, examining the core techniques, architectural patterns, and design trade-offs that practitioners face. Cutting across these paradigms, we examine two disciplines that shape every RAG system: context management, which governs how retrieved information is selected, compressed, and presented to the generator, and evaluation, which measures retrieval quality, generation faithfulness, and end-to-end system performance. To make techniques comparable across paradigms, we ground each in a shared vocabulary for the stages of a RAG pipeline and consolidate representative works along five recurring dimensions: retrieval stage, generation stage, system properties, trust and governance, and adaptability. Our analysis reveals that significant challenges persist. Hallucination is reduced but not eliminated, and retrieval augmentation can mask it from standard detectors. Retrieval quality remains highly sensitive to domain and query complexity. Effective use of long contexts lags behind the rapid growth of context window sizes. Automated evaluation metrics often diverge from real-world user satisfaction. We discuss these open problems alongside promising research directions, including multi-modal and federated architectures, cost-efficient graph systems, and standardized governance frameworks. Together, this survey offers a structured road map for researchers and practitioners navigating this rapidly evolving field.

candidates.title: DeRAG-Oracle: A Decentralized Retrieval-Augmented Generation Architecture for On-Chain Risk Telemetry
candidates.abstract: Smart contracts on the Ethereum Virtual Machine (EVM) cannot natively access unstructured enterprise data due to prohibitive on-chain storage costs and the lack of native text-parsing capabilities. Existing oracles remain bottlenecked by their reliance on strictly deterministic, structured data feeds. We propose DeRAG, a decentralized oracle architecture combining BNB Greenfield object storage, a FastAPI middleware powered by the Google Gemini Large Language Model (LLM), and Chainlink's Custom Runtime Environment (CRE). DeRAG distills complex, unstructured enterprise data into ultra-compact structured payloads that provide a deterministic representation of the probabilistic underlying inference, which can then be securely pushed to on-chain smart contracts. Evaluated over N=30 iterations, the architecture achieved a 100.0% execution success rate with a mean execution latency of 6.882 seconds, reducing raw enterprise data into average payloads of 369.43 bytes. By shifting heavy computation and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) off-chain, we demonstrate a robust bridge between enterprise data and Web3, enabling stable intelligence delivery designed to minimize on-chain data footprint.

candidates.title: SPARK: Simple Post-training for Adapting pRetrained Knowledge to Robot Control
candidates.abstract: Large-scale representation learning has produced public foundation models that provide strong general-purpose visual features. However, their pretraining objectives are not designed for robot representation learning, so the resulting embeddings tend to emphasize global semantics rather than the temporally sensitive representations required for robot control. Training robot models from scratch is also undesirable due to the limited scale and high collection cost of robotics data, as well as the substantial computational burden of pre-training. In this paper, we propose SPARK (Simple Post-training for Adapting pRetrained Knowledge), a post-training method that adapts foundation models to robot control. SPARK is built on two principles: temporal abstraction, which encourages the encoder to derive compact features that preserve information essential for understanding temporal changes and action-relevant scene structure, and knowledge preservation, which aligns patch-level representations with those of the original foundation model to retain useful pretrained semantics. These objectives yield compact visual state representations that remain semantically meaningful while preserving useful prior knowledge. Experiments across multiple robotics benchmarks show that SPARK consistently improves success rates and generalization over vanilla foundation models, and further demonstrate that these gains transfer to real-world robot manipulation.

candidates.title: Propagating Dataset Watermark for Black-Box Multi-Modal Retrieval Augmented Generation Services
candidates.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is an important technique for enabling LLMs to utilize proprietary multi-modal datasets. Due to limited local computational resources, RAG services are commonly outsourced to third-party providers. However, the black-box nature of these services provides data owners with little transparency into how their data are accessed and utilized. As a result, it becomes challenging to verify whether the entrusted data are improperly reused in unauthorized systems or fully incorporated into the target service, posing significant risks to both the intellectual property and the service quality of valuable data assets. In this paper, we propose a unified framework based on propagating dataset watermarking (PDW) to audit data ownership and utilization integrity in fully black-box multi-modal RAG services. PDW embeds imperceptible signals into the database and activates them through query probes, allowing their effects to propagate through retrieval and generation to verify actual data usage. By modeling probe responses probabilistically, our framework enables hypothesis testing with theoretical guarantees for data auditing. Experiments on two public datasets, four retrieval models, and four LLMs demonstrate that, even under adversarial settings, our framework can reliably identify partial and unauthorized database usage while incurring negligible impact on overall performance.

candidates.title: VIGOR: Benchmarking Visual Rationale Correctness in Multimodal Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are typically evaluated by whether they produce correct answers, but correctness alone does not reveal whether their outputs are supported by the right visual evidence. We introduce VIGOR, a benchmark for evaluating VIsually GrOunded Rationales in MLLMs. VIGOR represents visual rationales as explicit concepts paired with pixel-level groundings, covering multiple abstraction levels including low-level visual properties, intermediate structures, objects, parts and high-level motion, relations. To construct VIGOR at scale, we develop an automatic annotation framework that reuses existing dense supervision when available and generates missing concept groundings through proposal-based annotation followed by conservative multimodal verification. Using VIGOR, we evaluate whether MLLMs "look at what they say" by comparing model-derived visual evidence for each expressed concept against annotated ground-truth rationales. Our results show that current MLLMs exhibit limited visual rationale correctness and reveal distinct grounding failures across concept levels. VIGOR provides a benchmark and scalable data construction pipeline for studying whether MLLM outputs are supported by appropriate visual evidence. Code is available at https://github.com/deep-real/VIGOR

candidates.title: Text Steganography with Dynamic Codebook and Multimodal Large Language Model
candidates.abstract: With the popularity of the large language models (LLMs), text steganography has achieved remarkable performance. However, existing methods still have some issues: (1) For the white-box paradigm, this steganography behavior is prone to exposure due to sharing the off-the-shelf language model between Alice and Bob. (2) For the black-box paradigm, these methods lack flexibility and practicality since Alice and Bob should share the fixed codebook while sharing a specific extraction prompt for each steganographic sentence. In order to improve the security and practicality, we introduce a black-box text steganography with a dynamic codebook and multimodal large language model. Specifically, we first construct a dynamic codebook via some shared session configuration and a multimodal large language model. Then an encrypted steganographic mapping is designed to embed secret messages during the steganographic text generation. Furthermore, we introduce a feedback optimization mechanism based on reject sampling to ensure accurate extraction of secret messages. Experimental results show that the proposed method outperforms existing white-box text steganography methods in terms of embedding capacity and text quality. Meanwhile, the proposed method has achieved better practicality and flexibility than the existing black-box paradigm in some popular online social networks.

candidates.title: Spectral Rank and Step-Direction Dynamics in Language-Model Post-Training
candidates.abstract: Language-model post-training modifies weights through cumulative updates and successive displacements, yet existing studies report seemingly conflicting spectral properties: nearly full-rank updates and low stable-rank changes. We show these observations are compatible and characterize update directions during training. For singular values following $σ_i \propto i^{-α}$ with $0 < α\leq 1/2$, we prove that stable rank becomes negligible relative to fixed-energy rank as dimension increases. Full singular value decompositions of selected OLMo-2-7B updates confirm this separation: three proximal policy optimization (PPO) attention updates have stable ranks of 9.6-18.3 but require 532-1,222 singular components to capture 80% of their energy. We next compute consecutive checkpoint-displacement cosines from full-model inner products. Across nine publicly released reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards (RLVR) stages, all 131 adjacent pairs have negative cosines on their native checkpoint grids, including PPO and Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) trajectories. Supervised fine-tuning comparisons across four model families show configuration-dependent alignment, including negative late-training cosines for Mistral and FP32 Llama. Finally, a controlled OLMo-2-1B study with three paired seeds and a 2,048-token response cap compares group-relative advantages against a learned critic with generalized advantage estimation (GAE). At matched 60-rollout windows, late-training mean cosines are +0.259 and +0.012, respectively; the paired critic-minus-group difference is -0.247 (seed-level 95% interval [-0.358, -0.137]). These findings distinguish spectral concentration, energy coverage, and trajectory direction, and demonstrate that the advantage system influences directional alignment under matched training conditions.

candidates.title: Multi-Branch Policy Optimization for Multimodal Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Group-based reinforcement learning methods for multimodal large language models typically rely on trajectory-level credit assignment that applies a single advantage to all tokens in a response. However, multimodal reasoning involves substantially higher perceptual uncertainty than text-only settings: the model must repeatedly re-examine visual information to verify intermediate interpretations, while different visual groundings can lead to divergent reasoning paths. Consequently, such uniform credit assignment is particularly inadequate and causes relative advantages to progressively degenerate toward zero. To address these challenges, we propose Multi-Branch Policy Optimization (MBPO), a tree-based framework that constructs reasoning trees at vision-language decision boundaries, enabling sibling branches to explore diverse visual hypotheses and assigning segment-level credit through branch-relative advantages. We further introduce a temporal replay buffer to reuse informative segments while controlling policy staleness. Experiments on several multimodal reasoning benchmarks show that MBPO outperforms representative baselines, improving both learning signal quality and optimization efficiency. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/ShuaiLyu0110/MBPO.

candidates.title: Mitigating Visual Hallucinations via Evidence-Guided Multi-Image Reasoning in Visual Retrieval-Augmented Generation
candidates.abstract: Visual Retrieval-Augmented Generation (VRAG) has emerged as a promising paradigm for equipping Vision-Language Models (VLMs) with external visual evidence, enabling them to go beyond parametric knowledge when answering visually grounded questions. However, in such multi-image settings, VLMs still often suffer from visual hallucinations and struggle to accurately identify the question-relevant evidence needed for reliable reasoning. Existing methods usually lack an explicit cross-image evidence collection process, and also provide limited credit assignment when jointly optimizing perception and reasoning. To address this issue, we propose EVisRAG, an evidence-guided visual retrieval-augmented framework for multi-image reasoning. EVisRAG first observes the retrieved images, records question-relevant visual evidence from each image, and then performs reasoning and answer generation based on the aggregated evidence. We further introduce RS-GRPO, which aligns reward signals with token spans from different stages, improving training stability and strengthening the joint optimization of evidence localization and reasoning. Experiments on multiple visual question answering benchmarks show that EVisRAG consistently outperforms the backbone VLM by an average of about 19%, while substantially reducing visual hallucinations. These results demonstrate that explicit evidence collection and scoped reward design are effective for improving visual grounding and reasoning reliability in multi-image settings. Codes and data are available at https://github.com/OpenBMB/VisRAG.

candidates.title: HalluScope: Fine-grained Hallucination Diagnosis for Multimodal Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Although Multimodal Large Language Models have achieved strong performance across a wide range of vision-language tasks, they still suffer from hallucinations, where model outputs become inconsistent with the visual content, textual context, or commonsense knowledge. Existing studies primarily address this problem through coarse-grained detection. However, these approaches often provide insufficient diagnostic information for understanding hallucination types and supporting downstream hallucination mitigation. To bridge this gap, we propose fine-grained hallucination diagnosis for MLLMs, a new unified task that jointly performs hallucination detection, classification, and interpretable explanation generation. We develop an automated data generation pipeline and construct HalluScope-30K, a large-scale diagnostic dataset covering eight sources and five task categories. Based on this dataset, we design a multi-granular joint reward function and train two diagnosis models, HalluScope-4B and HalluScope-8B, which achieve state-of-the-art performance on both the MHALO benchmark and our fine-grained hallucination classification benchmark. Notably, detection and classification are mutually beneficial under joint optimization. Furthermore, diagnosis-driven feedback experiments show that the fine-grained diagnostic explanations produced by our model effectively guide target models to correct their hallucinations, with full diagnosis substantially outperforming all baselines on both Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct and LLaVA-1.5-7B. Our code, data, and models are available at https://github.com/wkinglin/HalluScope.

candidates.title: HRaLLM: Hyperbolic Rough Aware Large Language Model for Multimodal Action Reasoning
candidates.abstract: Multimodal action reasoning is a challenging problem due to redundant backgrounds, occlusions, viewpoint changes, etc. Existing approaches typically rely on either image or skeleton alone and fail to jointly model scene context and 3D human actions. To achieve action reasoning more accurately, we construct an unconventional multimodal large language model (MLLM) that employs compact skeleton manifold rough embeddings to complement defective image inputs sufficiently. Specifically, a novel rough tokenizer on hyperbolic manifold is proposed to learn hierarchical local-global geometric topologies of 3D skeleton sequences to build a comprehensible motion vocabulary for MLLM. Furthermore, to mitigate hallucination risks caused by cross-modal noise, we introduce a skeleton-image complementary fusion method that dynamically aligns and synchronizes multimodal information. Finally, we design meticulously a multimodal anticipation enhancement fine-tuning strategy based on a four-stage training paradigm to enhance spatio-temporal action reasoning capacity of MLLM effectively. Extensive experiments and visualization analysis demonstrate the outperformance of our MLLM across diverse benchmarks.

candidates.title: Geo3R: Mitigating Spatial Reasoning Hallucination in Multimodal Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Despite remarkable progress in visual understanding, Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) remain prone to hallucinations when reasoning about spatial relationships, often producing judgments that contradict the true 3D structure of the scene. Though several existing works have proposed to mitigate hallucinations, our analysis indicates that they show limited effectiveness in spatial reasoning, as they fail to bridge the fundamental gap between 2D visual representations and 3D spatial reality. Based on this finding, we define hallucinations arising from insufficient spatial structure modeling as spatial reasoning hallucination, a subcategory of relation hallucination that existing mitigation methods fail to address. We further identify three typical scenarios where such hallucinations frequently occur: perspective effects, object orientation, and viewpoint changes. To this end, we propose Geo3R, a training-free, plug-and-play framework that incorporates geometric evidence and structured 3D reasoning to mitigate spatial reasoning hallucination. Experiments on three benchmarks, covering 18 tasks across all three scenarios, show that Geo3R substantially reduces spatial reasoning hallucination across diverse MLLMs without additional training, outperforming existing models and methods. Code is available at https://github.com/hiMyee/Geo3R-Mitigating-Spatial-Reasoning-Hallucination.

candidates.title: Decoding the Delta: Unifying Remote Sensing Change Detection and Understanding with Multimodal Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: While Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) excel in general vision-language tasks, their application to remote sensing change understanding is hindered by a fundamental "temporal blindness". Existing architectures lack intrinsic mechanisms for multi-temporal contrastive reasoning and struggle with precise spatial grounding. To address this, we first introduce Delta-QA, a comprehensive benchmark comprising 180k visual question-answering samples. Delta-QA unifies pixel-level segmentation and visual question answering across bi- and tri-temporal scenarios, structuring change interpretation into four progressive cognitive dimensions. Methodologically, we propose Delta-LLaVA, a novel MLLM framework explicitly tailored for multi-temporal remote sensing interpretation. It overcomes the limitations of naive feature concatenation through three core innovations: a Change-Enhanced Attention module that systematically isolates and amplifies visual differences, a Change-SEG module utilizing Change Prior Embedding to extract differentiable difference features as input for the LLM, and Local Causal Attention to prevent cross-temporal contextual leakage. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Delta-LLaVA decisively outperforms leading generalist MLLMs and specialized segmentation models in complex change deduction and high-precision boundary localization, establishing a unified framework for earth observation intelligence.

candidates.title: ChemInsight: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Evaluating and Diagnosing Chemistry Understanding and Reasoning in Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: We introduce ChemInsight, a benchmark designed to evaluate large language models (LLMs) on chemistry tasks that require multi-step reasoning and structured chemical understanding. We propose a two-dimensional scoring system (scope and depth) to assess both task coverage and reasoning completeness. ChemInsight consists of 203 challenging chemistry questions organized into 50 bundles, which support the two-dimensional scoring evaluation scheme. We evaluate ten representative LLMs using ChemInsight and observe consistently low performance across models, with scope scores below 30% and depth scores below 11%, substantially lower than human expert performance. We then proceed to ask (1) What factor limits the advancement of current LLMs in chemistry? (2) To what extent are statistically driven language-model training methods effective at modeling chemistry symbolic language such as SMILES? And (3) Can LLM performance in chemistry be improved through intensive training on large, domain-specific corpora?

candidates.title: Capturing Token Tendencies for Training-Free Token Pruning in Multimodal Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: While visual token pruning is essential for efficient Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs), existing training-free methods suffer from a critical limitation: they rely on static, instantaneous heuristics to perform irreversible filtering. This approach ignores the hierarchical nature of MLLMs, where token importance often evolves dynamically rather than remaining fixed across layers. Consequently, tokens essential for deep-layer reasoning are often prematurely discarded by shallow-layer estimates. To address this, we propose Trend-aware Pruning, a novel framework that elevates pruning from a local snapshot decision to a temporal trajectory modeling problem. Instead of relying on isolated scores, our method captures the momentum of attention flow. This enables a dynamic rectification mechanism that selectively reactivates ''late-blooming'' tokens---those initially undervalued but exhibiting rising semantic importance---thereby preventing the loss of critical visual cues. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our approach achieves a superior efficiency-performance trade-off across diverse multimodal tasks. Notably, it reduces visual tokens by over 77.8%, retaining only approximately 23 tokens in the final layer while maintaining competitive performance, offering a robust and reversible solution for high-efficiency multimodal inference. The project page is available at https://github.com/JieMaMagic/Trend-aware-Pruning

candidates.title: Beyond the Logits: Mitigating Hallucinations in Multimodal Large Language Models with Layer-Adaptive Visual Guidance
candidates.abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have shown remarkable capabilities, yet they are prone to visual hallucinations: generating text that contradicts visual evidence. A prominent mitigation method is Contrastive Decoding (CD), which enhances visual guidance by penalizing logits derived from a visual-degraded context. Nevertheless, this approach is fundamentally limited as it relies only on the final output logits, ignoring intermediate layers' visual patterns which are crucial for alleviating hallucinations. To delve into this issue, we conduct a diagnostic dissection to trace the visual patterns within the intermediate layers. We quantify visual guidance strength at each layer via measuring the divergence between the predicted distributions from a full multimodal context and those from a visual-degraded context. Our analysis yields a critical insight: the visual guidance strength is adaptive across layers. In particular, the strength peaks in the middle layers and is surprisingly attenuated or even absent at the final layer. With such findings, we propose Layer-Adaptive VIsual Guidance (LAVIG), a novel training-free decoding algorithm to mitigate hallucinations in MLLMs. LAVIG directly adopts the layerwise visual guidance strength to adaptively re-weight visual tokens for the subsequent layer's self-attention computation. As a model-agnostic strategy, LAVIG can be seamlessly integrated into various MLLMs. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate that LAVIG sets a new state-of-the-art on major hallucination benchmarks, evidently reducing factual errors with marginal computational overhead. Code is available at: https://github.com/HiDream-ai/LAVIG/.

candidates.title: Alignment-Preserving Knowledge Transfer for Heterogeneous Multimodal Large Language Model Merging
candidates.abstract: Data-free model merging offers an attractive way to consolidate multiple Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) into a single system without retraining, reducing deployment cost while potentially combining complementary multimodal capabilities. However, existing heterogeneous MLLM merging methods primarily focus on mergeability under architectural heterogeneity while overlooking a more fundamental issue: preserving multimodal alignment. Here, multimodal alignment refers to the coordination between visual encoding and language reasoning encoded in language-side parameters. As a result, source information may be transferred along incompatible directions, silently disrupting vision--language coordination even when local parameter matching appears reasonable. To address this challenge, we propose APT-Merging, a strictly data-free alignment-preserving knowledge transfer framework for heterogeneous MLLM merging. APT-Merging comprises three key components: (1) a subspace extraction strategy based on truncated SVD that exposes the alignment-critical directional structure of the original model; (2) a dynamic mapping mechanism that aligns source components with compatible directions in the original model while filtering directionally incompatible information; and (3) a protective injection scheme that transfers only reliability-gated positive surplus along singular directions supported by the original model, thereby preventing off-subspace perturbations and reducing negative transfer. Extensive experiments on two heterogeneous MLLM settings and eight vision-language benchmarks demonstrate that APT-Merging achieves the strongest overall performance among compared data-free baselines. Further ablations show that alignment preservation is the most influential factor in achieving robust heterogeneous MLLM merging.

candidates.title: Benchmarking language models and agents for scientific reasoning in evolving materials laboratories
candidates.abstract: Large language models and the multi-agent systems built around them could accelerate materials discovery by connecting scientific knowledge with experimental decisions. Existing benchmarks establish capabilities in domain knowledge, multimodal interpretation and scientific tool use. As language models increasingly support materials research workflows, their ability to distinguish closely related material states and reason accurately with quantitative evidence remains insufficiently evaluated. These abilities are essential for comparing material responses, assessing mechanisms and maintaining reliable judgements as experimental evidence accumulates. We introduce MatScope to evaluate three connected capabilities. M1 tests unaided, condition-specific reasoning through 200 tasks spanning ten research functions, using aluminium and high-entropy alloys as representative material systems. M2 tests agent-assisted transfer of related knowledge to unresolved materials questions. MatEvoBench-20 tests initial forecasts across scientific dependency chains and revisions of still-hidden responses as observations accumulate. Across eleven model deployments, including GPT-6 Astra and Claude Fable 5.1, given-input calculations and many physical explanations are handled well. Fine-grained response estimates, comparisons between similar states and quantitatively supported choices remain substantially weaker. Related literature improves selected estimates, while condition and baseline mismatches limit transfer. Progressive observations calibrate some downstream responses and destabilize earlier accurate predictions. MatScope establishes measurable targets for developing reliable scientific reasoning in future self-evolving materials laboratories and materials-aware world models.

candidates.title: ViSR-KGC: Visual Subgraph Reasoning with Vision-Language Models for Multimodal Knowledge Graph Completion
candidates.abstract: Knowledge graph completion (KGC) aims to infer missing entities or relations from incomplete graph structures, and has evolved into multimodal knowledge graph completion (MMKGC), where entities are associated with multiple modalities such as text and images. Traditional representation learning approaches follow the embedding-based paradigm and may struggle when relation-specific evidence is limited. Meanwhile, LLM-based reasoning methods typically linearize graph structures into textual prompts, which obscures structural topology and neglects vital visual information. While vision-language models (VLMs) excel at multimodal reasoning, they cannot natively interpret structured graph topology, particularly when it comes to knowledge graphs where nodes and edges carry complex semantics. To bridge this gap, we propose ViSR-KGC, a visual subgraph reasoning approach for KGC. It integrates three complementary capabilities to capture semantic correlations: identifying global topology dependencies via representation learning, analyzing local multimodal evidence using VLMs, and providing necessary commonsense knowledge inherent in pre-trained models. Based on learned multimodal embeddings, our framework first extracts a compact and query-aware subgraph from the MMKG. Then, this subgraph is transformed into a visually interpretable image using a layout strategy selected through empirical comparison. Finally, the visualized subgraph, entity images, textual descriptions, and candidate answers are combined into a unified prompt, enabling the VLM to infer the missing entity. Experimental results on two real-world MMKG datasets demonstrate that ViSR-KGC consistently outperforms traditional embedding-based models and state-of-the-art multimodal baselines. This highlights the unique advantages of jointly leveraging VLMs' visual perception and internal knowledge for structured reasoning, thereby paving the way toward deeper investigation into VLMs' capacity for semantic graph analysis. The full version including Supplementary Materials is available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05833.

candidates.title: SinkRouter: Sink-Aware Routing for Efficient Long-Context Decoding in Large Language and Multimodal Models
candidates.abstract: In long-context decoding for LLMs and LMMs, attention becomes increasingly memory-bound because each decoding step must load a large amount of KV-cache data from GPU memory. Existing acceleration strategies often trade efficiency for accuracy by relying on heuristic pruning that may discard useful information. At a deeper level, they also tend to indiscriminately preserve all high-scoring tokens, treat early tokens as indispensable anchors, or rely on heuristic head routing, reflecting an insufficient mechanistic understanding of the attention sink phenomenon. In this paper, we show that attention sinks correspond to a model-encoded initial-position state with distinctive key geometry and low-impact value updates. Counterfactual anchor and head-output interventions further indicate that detected sink computations can be skipped with negligible output distortion. Based on this insight, we propose SinkRouter, a training-free selective routing framework that detects the sink signal and skips computations that would otherwise produce near-zero output. To translate this mechanism into real-world acceleration, we develop a hardware-aware Triton kernel with block-level branching and Split-K parallelism. We conduct extensive evaluations on a diverse suite of long-context benchmarks, including LongBench, InfiniteBench, CVBench, MileBench, and MMVP, using both text-only and multimodal backbones such as Llama-3.1-8B, Llama-3.1-70B, Yi-9B-200K, LLaVA-1.5-7B, and LLaVA-1.5-13B. Across these settings, SinkRouter consistently improves decoding efficiency while maintaining competitive accuracy, and reaches 2.03× speedup with a 512K context. Code is available at https://github.com/streamer-AP/SinkRouter.

candidates.title: CoRe: A Comprehensive Framework for Cross-Image Comparative Reasoning in Vision-Language Models
candidates.abstract: Cross-image comparative reasoning remains challenging for vision-language models (VLMs), especially when correct prediction requires fine-grained attribute grounding and globally consistent reasoning. We present CoRe, a unified framework for this problem. CoRe includes: (i) CoRe-20K, a large-scale triplet-based training set automatically constructed from structured visual metadata through a multi-expert collaborative pipeline, covering counting, depth, distance, and spatial relations; (ii) TriSR, a structured reward framework that jointly supervises attribute grounding, judgment alignment, and triplet consistency under GRPO optimization; and (iii) CoRe-Bench, the first benchmark dedicated to fine-grained cross-image comparative reasoning. Experiments show that CoRe substantially outperforms existing VLMs on CoRe-Bench while remaining competitive on standard multimodal benchmarks, achieving a 28.2-point gain in partial accuracy over the strongest baseline.

candidates.title: Inference Validation for Regulated AI: A Governed Decision Pipeline for LLM Serving
candidates.abstract: Deploying large language models in regulated industries requires more than picking the fastest inference engine: it requires evidence that a configuration meets contractual and legal obligations before it serves a single customer request. We describe Runway, an internal validation harness built at MasterControl that builds a governed decision pipeline around NVIDIA AIPerf. The key insight is separating concerns: AIPerf provides the trusted measurement, while Runway provides the experiment design that comes before it and the compliance, cost, and audit decisions that come after. We describe the architecture and the storage model that makes caching and audit one mechanism. We report three findings from Runway sweeps: TensorRT-LLM and vLLM rankings invert with concurrency; a newer, pricier GPU instance can be the cheaper one per request; and speculative decoding behaves differently across engines under load, so engine configuration can outweigh engine choice.

candidates.title: A bespoke, token-efficient LLM inference pipeline for extracting polymer diffusion coefficients from scientific literature
candidates.abstract: Automated creation of actionable chemical datasets through large language model (LLM) interpretation of chemistry publications has become an engineering challenge rather than a frontier AI problem. We present Chemstractor , a bespoke extraction pipeline designed for use with open‑weight LLMs that can be executed locally on hardware typically available to university research environments. As a test case, the extraction techniques are applied to polymer diffusion coefficients, commonly used for the prediction of polymer molecular weights and for evaluating emerging universal calibration curves. The pipeline combines modern PDF parsing, table focused chunking, structured prompting, and an agent orchestrated calculator tool to handle mathematical transformations and reduce hallucinations. Chemstractor achieves strong performance, including a low hallucination rate, while maintaining extremely low token usage and requiring no paid API access. The methodology provides an accessible and efficient route to generating validated, analysis ready datasets and offers a template for extracting similarly complex scientific parameters in other domains.

candidates.title: TileQuant: Tile as the Precision-Allocation Unit for LLM Mixed-Precision Post-Training Quantization
candidates.abstract: Post-training quantization (PTQ) reduces large language model (LLM) deployment costs, but preserving quality requires accounting for uneven weight sensitivity. Uniform PTQ uses one weight bit-width, importance-aware PTQ adjusts scales or reconstructs weights within that width, and column-wise mixed precision retains selected columns at higher precision. However, sensitivity varies within columns, so whole-column retention also protects less sensitive weights, while runtime outlier detection adds decoding overhead. We therefore introduce TileQuant, a training-free framework that assigns precision to hardware-aligned 2D weight tiles. Offline calibration provides input-activation-aware scoring from forward statistics for lower calibration cost and gradient-informed scoring from loss sensitivity for stronger quality preservation. Within each projection's retention budget, the highest-scoring tiles remain at 16-bit and the rest use 8-bit. The resulting map guides reconstruction into compact weight buffers, which the kernel reuses for native integer and 16-bit computation with local accumulation to reduce memory traffic. Experiments show that TileQuant reaches 2.66x the original model's generation throughput. Across language modeling, reasoning, long-context retrieval, and question answering, it preserves quality and surpasses quantized and original models on multiple tasks. These results support selecting precision units that capture local sensitivity while enabling efficient hardware execution. The implementation is: https://github.com/HanzhiZhang-Ulrica/TileQuant

candidates.title: Verify Before You Fetch: Reliable KV Cache Compression for LLM Inference
candidates.abstract: Long-context applications, long-lived agents, and multi-agent systems require large language models (LLMs) to process and retain extensive information. In these settings, the KV cache can exceed GPU high-bandwidth memory (HBM) capacity, necessitating offloading to host memory, where CPU-to-GPU transfers can dominate inference latency. While KV cache compression can reduce data movement, query-agnostic compression that guarantees accurate attention for arbitrary queries is extremely challenging, if not impossible. We introduce VerKV, a hybrid approach that provides $(ε, δ)$ guarantees for approximating attention on any given query. VerKV maintains a compact set of query-agnostic pivotal tokens on the GPU, together with a token-level sketch of the full KV cache, while retaining the complete cache in CPU memory. We introduce a novel stochastic sampling procedure, PoissonComp, to select the pivotal tokens. At inference time, our proposed KVFetch algorithm uses the pivotal tokens and the sketch to estimate the relative error of the resulting attention computation. If the estimate satisfies a user-specified $(ε, δ)$ tolerance, inference proceeds without accessing host memory. Otherwise, VerKV performs query-aware retrieval to fetch additional tokens from the CPU, refining the attention computation to meet the required tolerance. Thus, VerKV enables attention with bounded approximation error while minimizing CPU-to-GPU transfers. We show that PoissonComp outperforms state-of-the-art approaches to KV cache compression. Combined with KVFetch, it achieves near-dense performance (90-100% of dense quality at 32K context length, averaged over RULER and LOFT), using Qwen3-4B, Qwen3.5-9B and Ministral-3-8B, while reducing the GPU memory footprint by 8-32x and keeping CPU-to-GPU memory fetches within 2-23% of the cache per generated token, depending on the model.

candidates.title: From Game Generation to Game Playing: Fully Automated Ability Training for Vision-Language-Action Models
candidates.abstract: Training vision-language-action (VLA) models to follow gameplay instructions across diverse games is limited by the cost of collecting demonstrations. We introduce a framework that automatically generates game environments and expert demonstrations. An LLM-powered agent uses game-building tools to construct executable environments and tasks targeting specified skills. Programmatic experts then use privileged simulator state to generate aligned instructions, rendered observations, and keyboard and mouse actions. We train our game policy, Script2Play, by post-training a 4B vision-language model with behavior cloning on 150.3 hours of synthetic Minecraft and Roblox gameplay, without human gameplay demonstrations or reinforcement learning. Evaluation on multiple public game benchmarks demonstrates that Script2Play follows gameplay instructions effectively and generalizes across game engines, highlighting the effectiveness of targeted synthetic supervision.

candidates.title: The Surprising Effectiveness of Deleting Weights in LLM Post-Training
candidates.abstract: How little of a pretrained large language model (LLM) has to change for it to acquire new capabilities? We find that zeroing fewer than 0.05% of its weights, with no other modification, matches full fine-tuning (FFT) at scale across three LLM post-training regimes: reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, supervised fine-tuning, and on-policy distillation. Our method, Deletion Tuning, learns a binary mask over the gate projection of transformer blocks. Two practical advantages follow: the trained mask is hundreds to thousands of times smaller than the corresponding FFT checkpoint, and Deletion Tuning forgets far less, which addresses a central challenge in continual learning. Under reinforcement learning, its prior-task accuracy stays near the base level while FFT, LoRA, and random sparse fine-tuning lose up to 5.4 points. To understand why masking alone suffices, we analyze the geometry of the learned weight changes under reinforcement learning using stable rank, spectrum drift, and principal-weight overlap. Compared with LoRA and random sparse fine-tuning, Deletion Tuning is closest to FFT across the three measures.

candidates.title: Predictive Retrieval Preparation for Retrieval-Augmented Generation: Anticipating Future Knowledge Needs and Precomputing Reusable Retrieval Resources
candidates.abstract: The increasing adoption of Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) has established external knowledge retrieval as an important component of modern large language model (LLM) systems. By combining parametric language generation with non-parametric external knowledge, RAG enables generative AI systems to access information that may be unavailable in model parameters or may require frequent updating. Nevertheless, conventional RAG architectures remain predominantly reactive: document retrieval, query processing, relevance ranking, and contextual preparation are generally initiated after a user request arrives. Although existing optimization techniques have improved retrieval efficiency through vector indexing, embedding reuse, caching, approximate nearest-neighbor search, and retrieval pipeline optimization, they do not necessarily address whether the knowledge resources required by future requests can be anticipated and prepared before those requests materialize. This paper introduces Predictive Retrieval Preparation for Retrieval-Augmented Generation (PRP-RAG), a conceptual framework that investigates whether future knowledge requirements can be predicted from historical user interests, ongoing research activities, emerging information trends, document relationships, and temporal behavioral signals. Rather than pre-generating complete answers, PRP-RAG focuses on preparing the knowledge and retrieval resources that future RAG requests are likely to require. Its architecture integrates predictive knowledge-demand modeling, future information requirement generation, proactive document acquisition, document parsing and segmentation, embedding precomputation, retrieval index preparation, candidate knowledge organization, and adaptive retrieval execution. A central component is a knowledge-resource reuse mechanism that distinguishes reusable underlying knowledge assets from query-dependent retrieval decisions. This distinction enables potentially valuable document representations, embeddings, metadata, and indexed knowledge resources to remain useful even when the initially predicted question does not occur. The framework further investigates cost-aware preparation scheduling, including the possibility of performing document processing and embedding computation during periods of relatively low GPU utilization, favorable electricity prices, or lower-cost cloud GPU availability. A unified optimization formulation is developed to evaluate the expected benefits of predictive knowledge preparation while accounting for prediction uncertainty, document acquisition, parsing, embedding computation, index construction, storage, maintenance, information freshness, and subsequent resource reuse. The paper establishes an experimental methodology for evaluating retrieval latency, knowledge preparation expenditure, retrieval quality, resource reuse, prediction accuracy, and total system cost. Particular attention is given to prediction-error-tolerant knowledge reuse, where prepared knowledge resources may provide value across multiple future requests rather than only the specific questions initially predicted. The proposed framework does not assume that proactive preparation is universally beneficial; its effectiveness depends on the predictability of future knowledge demand, the reusability of prepared resources, preparation expenditure, document freshness, and retrieval compatibility. By shifting the focus from predicting future answers to anticipating and preparing future knowledge requirements, PRP-RAG investigates a complementary direction for improving the computational efficiency and responsiveness of retrieval-augmented generative AI systems.

candidates.title: Knowledge Graph-based Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Schema Matching
candidates.abstract: Traditional similarity-based schema matching methods fail to resolve semantic ambiguities and conflicts in complex, domain-specific mappings due to a lack of commonsense and domain-specific knowledge. In parallel, large language models (LLMs) without sufficient background knowledge tend to hallucinate, further complicating schema matching. To overcome these limitations, we introduce KG-RAG4SM, a Knowledge Graph-based Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Schema Matching. This method integrates novel retrieval mechanisms, including LLM-based, vector-based, graph traversal-based, and hybrid techniques with advanced reranking schemes to extract the most relevant subgraphs from large external KGs. Our approach achieves superior results without requiring re-training, as evidenced by improvements of 39.79% in precision and 30.56% in F1 score over LLM-based state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods (e.g., Jellyfish-8B) on the MIMIC dataset, and enhancements of 69.20% in precision and 21.99% in F1 score over pre-trained language model (PLM)-based SOTA methods (e.g., SMAT) on the Synthea dataset. Additionally, KG-RAG4SM scales effectively across KGs from commonsense KGs to domain-specific ones, while its instruction-tuning knowledge exclusion component ensures truthful performance in end-to-end schema matching tasks despite the suboptimal relevance of KG context. Our empirical analysis and case studies from real-world scenarios show that the hallucination problem in LLMs for schema matching is well mitigated by our solution.

candidates.title: BRAT: Bounded Residual-Aligned Training for Stable Multi-Pass LLM Post-Training
candidates.abstract: Reinforcement learning for large language model post-training often reuses each batch of sampled rollouts for several gradient passes to amortize the cost of generation. Under such multi-pass reuse, existing objectives fail in different ways: unclipped updates collapse as the policy drifts away from the sampling policy, adding a negative baseline avoids collapse but reinforces every sampled response, and PPO-style ratio clipping cuts off gradients abruptly. We first ask why reuse is fragile. Measuring how well an update estimated from a small rollout group aligns with the KL-regularized target on held-out rollouts of the same prompts, we find that this alignment drops by nearly an order of magnitude from in-sample to held-out rollouts across three base models, suggesting that repeated passes largely overfit the sampled group. Motivated by this finding, we propose Bounded Residual-Aligned Training (BRAT), motivated by a proximal update toward a bounded reweighting of the sampling policy. BRAT assigns each token a gradient weight that decreases linearly with its probability ratio and vanishes at a trust-region boundary, and normalizes group-centered rewards by their maximum magnitude, keeping advantages zero-mean and bounded without extra hyperparameters. With four reuse passes, BRAT avoids training collapse, limits policy drift, and achieves higher average accuracy with lower seed variance on most benchmarks.

candidates.title: Large Language Models without QK-Normalization
candidates.abstract: Query-Key Normalization (QK-Norm) is widely adopted in modern large language models to control the growth of attention logits and improve training stability. However, query and key norms are not merely sources of instability. The query norm controls the sharpness of the attention distribution, while the key norm determines how strongly a token attracts different queries. These norms therefore carry token-specific information about attention selectivity and token importance. By normalizing both, QK-Norm suppresses this information. This raises a natural question: can we control query-key representations without discarding their sensitivity to magnitude? To address this question, we propose QK-MAP, a Magnitude-Aware Projection for constructing queries and keys. Rather than removing magnitude through normalization, QK-MAP transforms the input representation using multiple learnable frequencies, so that changes in magnitude are encoded as bounded phase patterns. This allows magnitude to be represented through phase and direction rather than vector length alone. Its periodic features have a fixed norm while remaining sensitive to magnitude changes, separating magnitude encoding from norm growth. Multiple frequencies further help distinguish magnitudes and reduce periodic ambiguity. Experiments across model scales from 190M to 7B parameters show that QK-MAP achieves lower training and validation loss than both Standard attention and QK-Norm. Further analyses show that QK-MAP preserves sensitivity to input scale, assigns less attention to the first token, and produces stronger attention contrast for relevant evidence in synthetic long-context tests. These results demonstrate that query-key scale can be effectively controlled without sacrificing token-specific magnitude information.

candidates.title: Two-Sided Conformal Evidence Sets for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
candidates.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) can surface passages that support a claim, contradict it, or fail to address it, yet existing calibrated grounding methods are typically one-sided and model only supporting evidence. We introduce Conformal Evidence Sets (CES), a two-sided framework that returns separate support and refutation sets with finite-sample inclusion coverage of at least $1-α$ on each side under exchangeability; a Bonferroni union yields joint coverage of at least $1-2α$. On labeled candidate pools from the contrastive VitaminC benchmark, CES closely tracks nominal coverage across $α\!\in\!\{0.05,0.10,0.15,0.20,0.30\}$, with maximum deviations of $3.0$ percentage points for support and $5.4$ for refutation, and reaches essentially the same empirical coverage--size frontier as a test-tuned fixed-threshold heuristic without any test exposure. Stress tests mark the boundary of that guarantee: under FEVER distribution shift both sides under-cover, by up to $12.7$ percentage points, and support-side group-stratified recalibration substantially reduces the support gap. Scorer swaps, hard-negative retrieval, cross-dataset transfer, and a live end-to-end pilot expose a clear separation: when exchangeability holds and relevant evidence is retrieved, evidence inclusion remains calibrated even with an imperfect scorer, whereas the support/refute verdict tracks scorer quality directly. Calibrated evidence coverage and reliable verdicts are therefore distinct properties and should be reported separately.

candidates.title: Global Context Guidance for Diffusion Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Diffusion large language models (LLMs) have recently emerged as a promising alternative to autoregressive LLMs, enabling parallel generation through iterative denoising. Recent guidance methods improve diffusion LLMs by introducing a weak model to guide the prediction of the base model during denoising. However, the influence of the weak model during denoising remains less clear, and computing its prediction requires an additional forward pass at each denoising step. We present in this paper an in-depth analysis of how diffusion LLMs use contextual information during denoising. Our analysis reveals that diffusion LLMs rely more heavily on local context while often underutilizing global context. Based on this observation, we introduce Global Context Guidance (GCG), a feature-space guidance method that enhances global-context utilization without constructing an explicit weak model. Extensive experiments on LLaDA-8B, Dream-7B, and LLaDA-1.5 across diverse benchmarks demonstrate that GCG consistently outperforms existing guidance methods, while incurring much lower inference overhead.

candidates.title: Benchmarking Membership Privacy Risks in Preference-Based LLM Post-Training
candidates.abstract: Modern language models are commonly adapted after pretraining to follow instructions, align with user preferences, and improve deployment behavior. Such post-training often relies on preference data from users, annotators, or model interactions, which may contain sensitive prompts, private responses, proprietary tasks, or confidential judgments. Understanding the privacy implications of this data is therefore essential. Membership inference attacks (MIAs), which test whether a record was used for training, are the de facto standard for empirical privacy auditing in machine learning. However, preference-based post-training changes the unit of membership: a training record contains a prompt, a preferred response, and a dispreferred response, rather than a single input-output sequence. Audits that ignore this structure can under-report leakage. We therefore introduce a benchmark protocol that adapts strong reference-model MIAs to complete preference records. Our protocol asks whether membership is exposed by either response alone, by the model’s preference between them, or by the two responses jointly. We find that auditing the response pair can reveal membership evidence missed when the record is reduced to a single score. Across three preference datasets, two model families, and seven post-training objectives spanning three post-training families, measured leakage depends strongly on both the audited record statistic and the training objective, with imbalanced risk between preferred and dispreferred responses. We further evaluate the impact of parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) and differential privacy (DP), finding widely varying privacy-utility trade-offs. Overall, preference-based post-training leaks in ways that standard single-response audits can miss, motivating formal privacy methods that protect complete preference records while preserving post-training utility.

candidates.title: AbductionBench: Benchmarking Abductive Reasoning in Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Abductive reasoning is the inference of plausible explanations for observed evidence. Evaluating this capability requires more than a single task: a system may need to generate an explanation, discriminate among competing hypotheses, revise its hypotheses as evidence arrives, or decide what evidence to seek next. Yet these capabilities are typically evaluated through isolated benchmarks with different task formulations and scoring procedures, so claims that a model is ``good at abduction'' may reflect only a narrow aspect of this capability. We introduce AbductionBench, a unified framework whose taxonomy characterizes abductive tasks. We instantiate this framework on 27 datasets spanning ten domains and evaluate eight LLMs from four model families evaluated on single-choice selection tasks. Beyond harmonizing heterogeneous tasks, AbductionBench separates final-answer evaluation from analysis of the observable reasoning traces and interaction histories produced alongside those answers. We analyze written traces as observable model outputs rather than faithful representations of internal computation, characterizing evidence use, hypothesis comparison, uncertainty, contradiction handling, and answer commitment. Jev matches or exceeds small LLMs when selecting among explanations over compact evidence but falls substantially behind on longer cases, suggesting that candidate discrimination and extended evidence integration place different demands on a system. In interactive tasks, the proportion of actions judged relevant declines at later steps, and a relevant first question is associated with a correct final answer; in the passive task, models rarely revise their initial hypothesis as new evidence arrives. Together, these findings highlight the value of evaluating abductive reasoning through both final answers and observable evidence use, hypothesis revision, and information gathering.

candidates.title: Selective Cooperative Perception via Blind Spot Reasoning and Agentic Dialogue with Vision-Language Models
candidates.abstract: Real-time cooperative perception (CP) in multi-agent traffic environments is highly resource-intensive, which posing scalability challenges for large-scale deployment. Efficiency can be significantly improved by selectively performing CP only in safety-critical scenarios and for key occluding objects. Vision-Language Models (VLMs) are well-suited for complex reasoning in dynamic and uncertain environments, making them a promising tool for this selective CP task. This study proposes a VLM-driven agentic framework for blind spot reasoning and dialogue-based CP. A mixed-model architecture is designed that integrates conventional object detection for stable perception, vision-language reasoning for identifying impactful occlusions, and a physics-based geometric module to align reasoning with real-world visibility constraints. The framework also incorporates a Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting mechanism to enhance interpretability and intent-aware decision-making. We collect real-world data from connected vehicles operating in urban traffic and compare the driving-critical blind spot identification and dialogue performance of four state-of-the-art VLMs. Experimental results demonstrate that our method achieves over 80% accuracy in driving-critical blind spot detection and over 90% success in dialogue-driven perception sharing. This work provides a scalable, interpretable, and bandwidth-efficient alternative to conventional CP pipelines, and offers new insights into agentic communication design for future connected traffic systems.

candidates.title: Lightfoot: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Exact, Model-Free Document Deletion
candidates.abstract: Graph-based retrieval-augmented generation (GraphRAG) improves multi-hop question answering, but deployed systems pay costs that research comparisons rarely measure: model calls at query time, building the graph, and removing documents correctly. We present Lightfoot, a GraphRAG system in which every entity, link, fact and synonym edge is a deterministic function of per-passage extractions that carry chunk-level provenance. Retrieval makes no language-model call, indexing makes one per passage, and deleting a document is a database transaction with no model calls: 14 seconds for 10% of an 11,402-passage corpus, after which the graph is identical to a fresh index of the surviving documents. On a corpus of near-duplicate names, HippoRAG 2's capped synonym lists leave 565 fewer edges than a rebuild, while Lightfoot remains exact. Under identical extraction, embedding and answer models on held-out questions of MuSiQue, 2WikiMultiHopQA and HotpotQA, Lightfoot is competitive with HippoRAG 2: with Holm-corrected paired tests it is better on MuSiQue at recall@5 and recall@10 (+4.8 and +5.5 points) and on 2WikiMultiHopQA at recall@10 (+3.4), and tied on HotpotQA, while HippoRAG 2 keeps a non-significant 3.0-point edge at 2WikiMultiHopQA recall@2. Seeding the walk from entities named in the question accounts for most of the 2WikiMultiHopQA gain. Answers tie on all three datasets, and the retrieval pattern holds with three larger embedders, up to Qwen3-Embedding-8B. The gain is not the reranker's: with the same cross-encoder, dense retrieval trails Lightfoot by 9.3 and 17.8 points recall@5 on the two multi-hop sets. Lightfoot also builds the cheapest index, 26-31% below HippoRAG 2; LightRAG needed 2,187 model calls and 3.7 hours for the same deletion, and fast-graphrag cannot delete.

candidates.title: CompositionEvidence: Controlling Geometric Evidence for Cinematic Composition Reasoning with Frozen Vision-Language Models
candidates.abstract: Cinematic composition questions depend on in-frame geometry that vision-language models (VLMs) use inconsistently. External perception tools can expose this geometry, but naive prompt injection can overwrite useful visual predictions. On ShotBench composition, pre-question geometry reduces Qwen2.5-VL-7B from 49.5% to 46.3%; corrupted measurements lower it to 33.6%. CompositionEvidence derives nine reproducible features from frozen detection, depth, and line experts and supplies their shared 24-dimensional representation through two interfaces. A training-free channel appends gated neutral evidence after the question, reaching 56.2% (+6.7, exact McNemar p=0.0018) and 48.4% under corrupted evidence. A minimal-training channel maps the same representation to four soft tokens with a 7.37M-parameter projector while leaving the VLM frozen; it reaches 61.0% (+11.5). Across nine VLMs, including five commercial models queried through official provider APIs, zero-shot accuracy ranges from 43.8% to 63.0%, and the text channel changes it by +6.7 to -6.9 points; the highest baseline is among the regressions. The effect of explicit geometry depends on measurement reliability and on how the receiving model integrates it.

candidates.title: Efficient LLM Adaptation with Forward-Only Passes
candidates.abstract: Large language model (LLM) inference serving is undergoing rapid growth and large-scale deployment, motivating us to rethink how the inference process itself can be leveraged to enable efficient task-specific LLM adaptation. In this paper, we propose a forward-only approach for efficient LLM adaptation with forward-only passes in LLM inference serving. We exploit the angle concentration of activations induced by each singular value decomposition (SVD) component to measure its contribution-dispersed or concentrated-to the angle concentration of the hidden states. Based on this, our forward-only search then efficiently identifies the weight matrix with the highest dispersion that merits rank reduction. We then selectively remove the higher-order components and retain the lower-order components in SVD. Empirical results across diverse datasets demonstrate the competitive accuracy of our forward-only approach, while theoretical analysis shows lower peak memory and greater speedup than the gradient-based approach and greater speedup than the exhaustive search approach. The experiments further present the robustness and generalization of our forward-only approach to various LLMs with up to 57B parameters. The code is included in the supplementary material.

candidates.title: Depth-bounded reasoning in small language models: failures, defaults and the "No" fallback
candidates.abstract: We test how two small reasoning models (qwen3 1.7B and 4B, thinking mode) fail on logic puzzles whose difficulty is set by their depth in depth-bounded Boolean logic, i.e. the number of nested case splits a proof needs. We ask whether failures are wrong derivations or default answers, and whether a model that cannot settle a puzzle, and is not allowed to say so, falls back on "No" rather than "Yes".

candidates.title: OP-CL: On-Policy Guided Continual Post-training for Multimodal Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Continual post-training is essential for adapting Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) to evolving tasks, but it often leads to catastrophic forgetting. The core challenge is to achieve rapid adaptation to new task formats and semantics while preventing policy drift from accumulating into forgetting during sequential training. Existing paradigms address this trade-off only partially: Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) enables rapid adaptation but often disrupts prior knowledge, whereas Reinforcement Learning (RL) better preserves existing capabilities through on-policy updates but typically converges slowly and struggles on open-ended tasks. We propose OP-CL, a two-stage on-policy guided framework for continual post-training in MLLMs. In Stage 1, On-Policy Corrective Supervision transforms model rollouts into corrective supervision, providing efficient learning signals for acquiring new-task behaviors, especially on open-ended tasks. Since such rapid adaptation may still introduce policy deviation, Stage 2, Reward-KL Stabilized Reinforcement further stabilizes continual adaptation by adaptively regulating KL regularization to limit excessive policy updates. The two stages therefore address two complementary requirements of continual post-training: efficient acquisition and stable retention. Experiments show that OP-CL consistently achieves a better balance between new task adaptation and old task retention than representative SFT- and RL-based baselines.

candidates.title: MINE: Entropy-coded Memory-efficient Inference for Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: We present MINE (Memory-efficient INference Engine), a lossless entropy coding approach that accelerates single-stream inference of Large Language Models (LLMs), where existing lossless compression methods yield speedups only for specific data types such as BF16 and under additional assumptions. Single-stream decoding is strongly memory-bound, since every weight must be streamed from memory once per generated token and requests cannot be batched in local or low-latency deployments. At the core of MINE is dtANS-LLM, a GPU entropy coding scheme adapted from the prior dtANS to the needs of LLM inference. It exploits the non-uniform distribution of weights, which persists even after quantization, and exposes hyper-parameters that trade compression ratio against decoding cost. We auto-tune these parameters for each tensor and GPU to obtain the Pareto front between model size and decoding latency. MINE integrates into vLLM as a plugin and selects the best kernel configuration for a given memory budget. On Llama 3.1 8B Instruct with a 2.1-bit EntQuant checkpoint, MINE achieves speedups of 2.52x and 1.48x over the fastest baseline on an RTX 4060 Ti and an RTX 5090, at effective bitrates of 2.24 and 3.43 bits per weight. MINE is available as open source.

candidates.title: A Social Choice Theory Approach Towards Quantifying Causal Reasoning in Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Large language models can answer causal questions correctly while relying on shallow associations, lexical cues, or familiar answer patterns rather than the causal structure described in the prompt. This makes causal reasoning an important target for trustworthy language-model evaluation, since output accuracy alone may not reveal whether a model will generalize reliably under distribution shift or in downstream decision-support settings. We present a white-box auditing framework that uses social choice theory to quantify the role of individual attention heads in causal prediction. Our hypothesis is that, if a model engages task-relevant causal structure, then a sparse subset of attention heads should become disproportionately pivotal when the prompt requires interventional or counterfactual reasoning rather than simple association. Treating attention heads as voters in a cooperative game, we estimate each head's Banzhaf power: how often the head is pivotal in shifting the model toward the correct ``yes'' or ``no'' answer on a causal task. We apply this method to CLadder, a benchmark spanning associational, interventional, and counterfactual reasoning, using Qwen-2.5-1.5B-Instruct, Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct, and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. We further compare Banzhaf-based pivotality with a gradient-based functional-specialization probe that identifies heads whose representations distinguish causal task types. Across models, both approaches reveal sparse, localized attention-head subnetworks concentrated mainly in middle and late layers. However, similar mechanisms appear in both correct and incorrect generations, suggesting that the models often detect the form of causal queries without reliably executing the required causal reasoning. The Banzhaf and gradient methods highlight overlapping but distinct heads, suggesting complementary roles for representational encoding and final answer routing. By converting internal model behavior into component-level evidence about answer-generation pathways, this work contributes to AI assurance initiatives for foundation models. It supports more transparent evaluation and targeted testing of components and failure modes relevant to using LLMs inside larger AI-enabled systems.

candidates.title: Does Reasoning Improve Psychological Depth in Large Language Models?
candidates.abstract: Benchmark gains from reasoning-enhanced large language models encourage the assumption that these models should broadly perform better on complex generative tasks, but this remains underexplored in open-ended, creative domains shaped by nuances of reader experience. We tested this assumption through the lens of psychological depth in short stories. We compared DeepSeek-R1 vs. DeepSeek-V3, our closest available contrast for reasoning-oriented post-training, and GPT-5 vs. GPT-4o, through 60 blinded pairwise evaluations in which seven human annotators and an ensemble LLM-as-a-Judge rated prompt-matched story outputs. Human evaluations showed no universal reasoning advantage: GPT-5 was slightly preferred over GPT-4o (60.0-62.9% across two reasoning-effort settings), whereas DeepSeek-R1 fell behind DeepSeek-V3 (42.9%). Although this pattern was marked by low inter-annotator agreement (Krippendorff's $α= 0.070$), our annotation-quality checks suggested genuine evaluative subjectivity, plausibly reflecting distinct annotator decision schemes rather than annotation failure. In contrast, the LLM-as-a-Judge showed a strong pro-reasoning bias (98.3% of pairs vs. 55.2% of human votes), consistent across its five configurations and partly tracking sentence length. These findings suggest that, at the frontier, reasoning-related quality differences are small enough to be dominated by reader subjectivity, and that LLM-as-a-Judge evaluators can obscure this subjectivity in nuanced creative-generation tasks.

candidates.title: What Does Hard-Negative Fine-Tuning Teach Multimodal Large Language Models? Controlled Evidence from a Compositional Benchmark
candidates.abstract: Fine-tuning on hard negatives is a popular way to improve the compositional reasoning of vision-language models, but when accuracy goes up it is rarely clear what the model actually learned. We ask this question for multimodal large language models. We use CompHall, 2,860 forced-choice questions (spatial, attribute, counting and part-whole) with two graded hard negatives each, three model families (LLaVA-1.5, LLaVA-NeXT and Idefics2), and controls that such studies often lack: gray-image evaluation, three seeds, option-order tests, control arms trained on different question types, and independent benchmarks. We find four things. First, CompHall is not a pure test of vision: part-whole questions can be answered from the text alone (66-95% without the image), and per-image accuracy is unrelated to an object-hallucination probe (r = -0.05), so we see no evidence that compositional failures drive hallucination. Second, the original fine-tuning method scored mostly image-placeholder tokens and hurt both LLaVA models. With a corrected loss, fine-tuning raises accuracy on the spatial-relation questions of CV-Bench in all three families, by +3.2, +23.1 and +6.0 points (averaged over both option orders). Control arms show that the gain needs spatial training questions, and for LLaVA-NeXT about two-thirds of it appears even on relation words that were only wrong options in training. Third, the gain is not general: on CompHall itself it is significant only for LLaVA-NeXT (+6.9 points) and not detectable for Idefics2, it reaches about 3 points at most on true/false statements, and LLaVA-1.5 fine-tuned on other question types learns to answer "true" too often. Fourth, both losses raise the yes-bias of LLaVA-1.5 on POPE.
